title: Free consent — coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake (ICA ss. 13–22)

content.overview: Consent is free when not caused by coercion (s. 15), undue influence (s. 16), fraud (s. 17), misrepresentation (s. 18), or mistake (ss. 20–22). Voidable contracts may be rescinded; bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement renders it void (s. 20).

sections.heading: Coercion and undue influence
sections.body: Coercion involves acts forbidden by penal law or unlawful detention of property to induce the agreement. Undue influence arises where one party can dominate the will of the other and uses that position.

sections.heading: Fraud and misrepresentation
sections.body: Fraud is intentional deception within s. 17. Misrepresentation covers unwarranted statements and related s. 18 cases. Silence may amount to fraud where there is a duty to speak.

sections.heading: Mistake
sections.body: Section 20: bilateral mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement makes it void. Section 22: unilateral mistake of fact does not by itself make a contract voidable.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Pray rescission and restitution. Plead particulars of the vitiating factor — general fraud allegations fail.

illustrations: A threatens B with prosecution of B’s son unless B executes a bond; the statutory illustration to the coercion provision treats the resulting bond as avoidable at B’s option.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
India Code rule for sections 13–22: Sections 13–22 define consent and free consent and address coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation and mistake. Sections 19 and 19A provide the statutory consequences for agreements affected by specified vitiating factors.

Definition: Free consent exists when parties agree upon the same thing in the same sense and the consent is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or the mistake situations recognised by sections 20–22.

Ingredients / conditions:
1. Establish consent to the same thing in the same sense.
2. Identify the alleged vitiating factor and its statutory definition.
3. Prove the causal connection between that factor and the consent where required.
4. Apply the specific consequence under sections 19, 19A, 20, 21 or 22 rather than a general allegation of unfairness.
